chapter: Ornette, Los Angeles and the Marines
title: Hearing Dizzy Gillespie's band in 1949
summary: His first bebop experience is Dizzy's 1949 concert, segregated at Booker T. Washington auditorium.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Do you remember the first bebop tune you heard? Do you remember your reaction?

No. I don’t remember the first one. My reactions most of the time had to do with live performances. There was a radio show here for a while, maybe in the late 1940s, that did play more modern jazz, bebop. I would listen to it, but I didn’t really – it had a certain appeal to me, but I didn’t know what they were doing. The first bebop experience that I had was going to a concert and listening at that band that Dizzy had in ’49, that band. They came here. I said, that’s what I want to do, right there. I had a chance to talk to Dizzy about that. Boy, Dizzy was a nut.
’49. You would have been about 15. Pretty young. Talking to Diz about. Was he open? Was he receptive to . . . ?

I didn’t talk to him then. I talked to him later on. But I went to the concert. The concert was at the Booker Washington auditorium. Mixed concerts was forbidden. So Norman Granz say, we ain’t playing no segregated auditorium. So what he did, he brought the concert to Booker T. Washington High School auditorium, and they figured out how to segregate it anyway. That was kind of funny, in a way. Downstairs – and how I found out was sheer accident – I had a ticket for seat whatever it was, E-3 or whatever. All these white people were sitting around me. The cat said, “Man, let me see your ticket.” I showed it to him. He said, “Oh, it’s on that side” in the same row. That was when I heard that band, and I knew that that was what I really wanted to do. I didn’t know how I was going to do it, but I knew that that’s what I wanted to do.
